questions.question: Why should an ANN index be evaluated against exact nearest-neighbor results on representative queries?
options: Exact results provide the ground truth needed to measure recall@k
Exact search always has lower latency than ANN search
ANN indexes cannot return similarity scores
Exact search automatically enforces tenant authorization
questions.explanation: Recall@k asks how many exact top-k neighbors the approximate search recovered. Without an exact reference set, the team cannot quantify approximation loss.

questions.question: A query retrieves 40 global ANN candidates, but only 5% pass the tenant filter. The API needs 10 results. What is the main risk of post-filtering?
options: Candidate starvation can leave fewer than 10 authorized results
The embedding dimension changes after filtering
Cosine similarity becomes Euclidean distance
The write checkpoint moves backward
questions.explanation: At 5% selectivity, only about two of 40 candidates survive on average. Indexed pre-filtering or an adaptive retrieval plan is needed to protect both authorization and result count.

questions.question: Which HNSW query-time change usually trades more work and latency for higher recall?
options: Increase the search candidate list or search effort
Reduce every vector to zero dimensions
Remove the exact evaluation set
Generate a new point ID on every retry
questions.explanation: Exploring a larger candidate set gives the graph search more opportunities to recover true neighbors, at the cost of more distance work and latency.

questions.question: Why must the embedding model version, dimension, normalization, and distance metric be versioned together?
options: They define the vector space in which scores are meaningful
They determine the HTTP status code
They replace metadata authorization filters
They eliminate the need for a rollback index
questions.explanation: A query vector is comparable to indexed vectors only under the same representation contract. Mixing spaces can silently corrupt ranking even when the API stays healthy.

questions.question: A write is acknowledged but an immediate query does not return it. What must the API expose if the product requires read-after-write behavior?
options: A checkpoint or sequence that the read path can wait for or cover with an overlay
A larger top-k with no freshness signal
A random delay hard-coded in the client
A lower vector dimension
questions.explanation: A sequence or checkpoint turns freshness into an observable contract. The read path can wait until the serving index catches up or merge a bounded change overlay.

questions.question: How do stable point IDs, source versions, and tombstones work together during retries?
options: They deduplicate delivery, reject older mutations, and prevent deleted content from being resurrected
They make every ANN result exact
They remove the need for backups
They guarantee zero indexing latency
questions.explanation: Stable identity makes retries address the same record, version checks preserve ordering, and tombstones keep delayed writes from reviving revoked data.

questions.question: Which release evidence best shows that a vector-search change is safe?
options: Recall and ranking quality by slice, latency and throughput at load, freshness lag, filter correctness, and rollback readiness
Only the average query latency on an unfiltered synthetic vector
Only the number of vectors stored
Only the vendor's default configuration
questions.explanation: A production release must preserve retrieval quality, serving performance, data correctness, and recoverability across representative workload slices.
